title: Progressive Degradation and Tenant Throttling Playbook
author: Aisha Moreno
body:
Summary:
This playbook describes the recommended patterns, operator procedures, and automated controls for progressive degradation and tenant-level throttling in private (VPC/on‑prem) Redwood deployments. It provides a step-by-step runbook for safely limiting tenant resource consumption while maintaining the best possible service for remaining traffic. The goal is to keep high-priority requests healthy, preserve KV/LLM cache integrity where possible, and provide clear operator actions and rollback paths.

Scope and intent:
- Applies to private deployments (VPC and on‑prem control planes) running multi‑tenant inference nodes or shared service planes.
- Focus on non-destructive throttling (rate limits, concurrency caps, queueing and shed patterns) and progressive feature degradation (smaller model fallbacks, quantized execution, disabled non-critical features).
- Designed for both reactive incident response and pre-emptive autoscale-driven protective behaviors.

Key definitions:
- Tenant: customer namespace, logical tenant on the control plane.
- Progressive degradation: ordered, reversible reduction of functionality (e.g., disable long-context mode, reduce max_tokens) to reduce resource pressure.
- Throttling: controls limiting request rate, concurrency, token throughput.
- SLOs referenced: 99th percentile tail latency (p99), request success rate, and model correctness (measured by quality guards).

High-level strategy:
1) Detect: use telemetry to identify high-usage tenants or runaway traffic patterns.
2) Contain: apply per-tenant soft limits and backpressure to stop immediate pressure on shared resources.
3) Degrade progressively: move the tenant through an ordered set of fallbacks that trade capabilities for resource savings.
4) Observe: confirm reduction in pressure and validate critical customer flows remain functional.
5) Restore: rollback degradations in controlled stages after pressure normalizes.

Signals and thresholds (operator-visible):
- Metrics: tenant_request_rate, tenant_concurrent_sessions, tenant_tokens_per_minute, node_gpu_utilization_5m, kv_cache_hit_rate, p99_response_ms, error_rate_5m.
- Primary thresholds (tunable per deployment):
  - tenant_tokens_per_minute > 150k for 3 minutes => WARNING
  - tenant_concurrent_sessions > 250 for 2 minutes => WARNING
  - node_gpu_utilization_5m > 92% for 2 minutes => CRITICAL
  - p99_response_ms > 1200ms and error_rate_5m > 0.5% => CRITICAL

Escalation policy summary:
- WARNING: auto-notify tenant owner via configured contact; place tenant into soft-throttle mode (see automated controls).
- CRITICAL: escalate to oncall SRE (level-1) and apply controlled progressive degradation. Notify account team and CS.

Automated controls (order of operations):
1) Soft Throttle (non-terminating): impose 20% rate reduction via token-bucket enforcement at the edge.
2) Queueing with Priority: shift tenant to a priority queue with a 5s admission timeout; priority score based on SLA tier.
3) Feature Reduction Stage 1: disable optional tooling (e.g., embedding rerank, long-context KV-prefetch).
4) Feature Reduction Stage 2: cap max_tokens to 512 and reduce streaming chunk size.
5) Model Fallback Stage: route requests to a smaller, cheaper quantized variant (e.g., redwood-llama-quant-1) with explicit response header X-RD-Model-Fallback.
6) Burst-only Mode: allow short bursts but enforce a slow steady-state baseline (e.g., 10 requests/min).
7) Tenant Quarantine (last resort): soft-eviction (reject new sessions with 409 + JSON body linking to support) — only after manual approval.

Operator runbook: Immediate manual steps (for CRITICAL events)
1) Confirm alert context and affected tenants. Review dashboards: tenant_request_rate, tokens_per_minute, node_gpu_utilization (links in the incident header).
2) If node_gpu_utilization_5m > 92% and multiple tenants are impacted: trigger cluster-level autoscale (if allowed) or initiate tenant-level throttles.
3) For single high-usage tenant: set "soft_throttle" attribute on tenant in control plane. CLI example:

# Example CLI (Control Plane)
redwoodctl tenant update --tenant my-tenant-id --set soft_throttle=true --throttle-rate 0.8

4) After soft_throttle, monitor for 2 minutes. If no improvement, move to Feature Reduction Stage 1 using the control-plane flag set: reduce_prefetch=true.

# Example API call (internal control plane API)
PATCH /internal/tenants/my-tenant-id/degrade
Content-Type: application/json
{
  "stage": "feature_reduction_1",
  "reason": "high_gpu_utilization_critical_2026-06-10"
}

5) Continue through the stages as needed. Record each stage as an event in the tenant audit log with start_time, operator, and rationale.

Rollback and restore procedure:
- Preconditions: node_gpu_utilization_5m < 70% for 10 minutes and p99_response_ms within SLO for 15 minutes.
- Steps: reverse degradation stages in reverse order with 5–10 minute observation windows per step.
  1) Remove Tenant Quarantine flag. 2) Re-enable Model Fallback to primary model. 3) Incrementally increase max_tokens back to configured value. 4) Re-enable optional tooling (rerank/long-context). 5) Clear soft_throttle.

Safety and data integrity notes:
- Never perform state-destructive operations during degradation (no KV state truncation or forced cache evictions).
- When switching model variants, preserve model signature headers and surface a brief policy note to the tenant via X-RD-Degradation-Note so downstream integrators can detect fallback behavior.
- Audit logs must include operator id and change request id for compliance evidence.

SLO and acceptance criteria for degradation behavior:
- Under progressive degradation, p95 latency should remain <= 1.5x baseline and errors <= 2x baseline for the degraded tenant.
- Shared tenants should maintain 99% of baseline success rate.
- Observability: every degradation stage change must emit an event with tags {tenant_id, stage, operator}.

Testing and validation checklist (pre-production):
1) Synthetic workload: generate 3x normal tokens/minute from a single tenant for 15 minutes.
2) Verify soft throttle triggers and that edge rejects beyond configured rate.
3) Validate that model fallback route returns compatible schema and that downstream QA tests pass.
4) Run chaos test: induce node GPU saturation and confirm system moves tenants through degradation stages without state loss.

Configuration examples and snippets:
- Rate limit policy (example YAML for Envoy/edge):

policies:
  tenant_rate_limit:
    type: token_bucket
    params:
      capacity: 1000
      refill_tokens_per_sec: 5
      tenant_key: "%REQUEST_HEADER(tenant-id)%"
      soft_fraction: 0.8

- Control-plane degradation policy (example JSON flag set):

{
  "degradation_policy_v1": {
    "stages": [
      {"id": "soft_throttle", "actions": ["rate_reduce_0.8"]},
      {"id": "queue_priority", "actions": ["shift_to_queue(priority=low,timeout=5s)"]},
      {"id": "feature_reduction_1", "actions": ["disable_prefetch","disable_rerank"]},
      {"id": "feature_reduction_2", "actions": ["cap_max_tokens_512"]},
      {"id": "model_fallback", "actions": ["route_to:redwood-llama-quant-1"]}
    ]
  }
}

(Administrators: load the JSON as a policy with redwoodctl policy apply --file degradation_policy.json)

Operator checklist for drill and runbook validation:
- Ownership: oncall SRE (first responder) -> runtime team -> customer success for customer comms.
- Communication template: short incident message stating that tenant experienced temporary degraded performance due to resource pressure, include expected restore window and a link to the support ticket.

Communication escalation template (example):
- [Subject] Temporary Service Degradation for Tenant <tenant_name>
- [Body] We detected sustained GPU utilization and token throughput originating from your tenant. We put you into a temporary degraded mode (rounded list of actions) to protect overall cluster health. We will restore full service after utilization stabilizes. Contact support@example.redwood.com or your account rep for questions.

Audit and post-incident analysis:
- For every degradation incident, open an incident review doc and populate: root_cause, timeline (events and stage transitions), metrics pre/post, owner decision logs, and remediation actions.
- Required artifacts: tenant audit events export (.csv), relevant node telemetry window (1h), control-plane event log trace (trace-id).

Appendix A — Example sanity table for operator thresholds:
| Signal | Severity | Trigger | Immediate operator action | Auto-step | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| node_gpu_utilization_5m | CRITICAL | >92% x2 minutes | Check cluster, consider autoscale | Feature reduction 1 | If whole cluster saturated, prioritize golden tenants |
| tenant_tokens_per_minute | WARNING | >150k x3 minutes | Notify tenant owner, apply soft throttle | Soft Throttle | Tune per-customer in onboarding |
| p99_response_ms | CRITICAL | >1200ms & error_rate_5m>0.5% | Escalate to SRE, start degrade stages | Queueing | Correlate with node metrics |

Appendix B — Example observability query (Prometheus):
- High-usage tenant candidate:
  sum by (tenant_id) (rate(redwood_tenant_tokens_total[1m])) > 2500
- Node saturation window:
  max_over_time(node_gpu_utilization{job="runtime"}[3m]) > 0.92

Appendix C — Ownership and contacts:
- Primary oncall: runtime-sre rotation (see roster)
- Tier-1 support: customer-success-engagers@redwood.internal
- Runtime team lead: Priya Kothari
